title: Fats Waller: drinking in Los Angeles and his death
summary: Moore recalls drinking with Fats at the Lincoln Theater and his prophetic remark before dying on a train.

that we neglected to talk about from the '40s that you knew from the late '30s and '40s -- Fats Waller. We talked between us about him but we didn't really -- tell us some of your friendships with Fats. Oh, Fats, I wish I were he, on the road just like -- the corner of the road. But I ran into Fats a number of times -- In Denver, and up in Seattle and finally we got together at the Lincoln Theater in Los Angeles. He was appearing there and in between being on stage he and I would -- he loved Old Grand-Dad and during those years I could wail with my liquor, too. We were drinking, we would put away about three quarts of Grand-Dad, we were pretty loaded at that time and then we -- I said to Fats, "We can't carry on like this. We ain't going to be long for this world if we're going to carry on like this. Let's stop this mess." He says, "Well, maybe I'll take one more. Chief if I have to go, I want to go happy," he said. It was an ironic prophetic statement because in about three more months he was gone. He was on his way back to the east and he died in Kansas City on the train and that was the story of Fats and I knew him and I knew that Gene Sedric / for quite a while and also Slick Jones was the drummer and Johnny Bogg

was the trumpet player at one time. We had a beautiful thing going, that's where that play comes from, 'Aint Misbehavin' That's on Broadway now. I saw the play, it reminded me of my days that I knew Fats well. And I got many of his records here and whenever I want to laugh and carry on, I listen to 'Your Feets Too Big.' 'Dark Town Strutters Ball' with the corny horn on the taxi -- 'Taxi,' he was a happy man, he went happy.
When he was on earth -- beautiful.
